title: Training the Person Who Would Replace Me
script: Narrator: [warmly] When I learned that I would move to another department, my manager asked me to train Rafi to handle the weekly inventory report.
Narrator: At first, I planned to show him the spreadsheet once and send my old notes. I had done the task for two years and forgot how many steps were not written down.
Narrator: [thoughtful] During our first session, Rafi asked why one supplier's numbers were always checked separately. The reason existed only in my memory.
Narrator: We created a clearer guide together. It included the source files, order of checks, common errors, deadline, and person to contact for unusual cases.
Narrator: [carefully] I demonstrated one report while explaining my decisions. The next week, Rafi completed it while I watched silently.
Narrator: He made one mistake with returned items. Instead of taking the keyboard, I asked him to trace the total back to the source.
Narrator: [reflective] He found the problem and added a warning to the guide in his own words.
Narrator: For the third report, I reviewed only the final figures and questions. Rafi no longer needed me beside him.
Narrator: [honestly] We also asked another coworker to follow the guide. She found two instructions that were obvious to us but unclear to a new reader.
Narrator: Before my transfer, Rafi handled the full cycle and sent the report on time.
Narrator: [gently] Training did not mean proving that the task was difficult or showing every shortcut at once. It meant making another person safely independent.
Narrator: I kept access rules in place. Rafi received the accounts required for his role; I did not share my personal password.
Narrator: [encouraging] The manager stored the guide in a team folder with an owner and review date, so it would not become an old forgotten file.
Narrator: On my first day in the new department, nobody called me about inventory. That silence was evidence of a successful handover.
Narrator: [sincere] Good knowledge transfer leaves a process stronger than one person's memory.

quiz.question: What task would Rafi take over?
quiz.explanation: The narrator was transferring a repeated reporting duty.

quiz.question: What weakness appeared in the old process?
options: Important reasons existed only in memory
quiz.explanation: Two years of habit had hidden unwritten knowledge.

quiz.question: How did Rafi learn after the demonstration?
options: He completed a report while the narrator observed

quiz.question: Why did another coworker test the guide?
options: To find instructions unclear to new readers
quiz.explanation: A fresh reader revealed hidden assumptions.

quiz.question: What shows a successful handover?
options: The old worker stays necessary forever
The process works independently and safely
Only one person understands the task
quiz.explanation: Strong transfer reduces dependence on personal memory.

quiz.question: What hidden weakness does Rafi’s question reveal?
options: An important supplier check exists only in one person’s memory
The deadline is unknown to everyone

quiz.question: Why does the narrator avoid taking the keyboard?
options: Tracing the error helps Rafi learn the process independently

quiz.question: What does the third-party test reveal?
options: The report total is always wrong
Instructions obvious to the writers can confuse a new reader

quiz.question: Why not share a personal password?
options: Role-based access should be granted through proper accounts

quiz.question: What keeps the guide useful later?
options: A team owner and scheduled review date
